name: Majoritarianism
summary: Majoritarianism holds that the majority of a community, usually of its voters, has the right to decide collective questions, and that limits placed on that majority are suspect unless they only keep future majorities and minority participation possible. Its institutional form is the Westminster model of single-party majority government, plurality elections and a flexible constitution, and its philosophical form is the case that courts and entrenched rights should not override elected legislatures. Beyond decision procedure it has no program, so most economic and cultural questions are left to whatever majority forms.
scope: The mainstream procedural and institutional strand: Locke's majority-consent argument, Lijphart's majoritarian (Westminster) model as opposed to consensus democracy, and Waldron-style objections to judicial review as summarised in scholarship and Wikipedia. It excludes ethnic or religious majoritarianism, which defines the majority by identity and would answer identity-related statements differently. Because the doctrine is about how decisions are made, many policy statements are answered 0 with low confidence.

keyFigures.name: John Locke
keyFigures.role: Argued that the act of the majority binds the whole political community.

keyFigures.name: Jeremy Waldron
keyFigures.role: Legal philosopher who argues that majority decision by legislatures is more legitimate than judicial review.

keyFigures.name: Arend Lijphart
keyFigures.role: Political scientist who defined the majoritarian (Westminster) model as the contrast to consensus democracy.

universal-healthcare.rationale: Majority rule is a decision rule, not a welfare program; adherents would let the majority decide healthcare either way.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: Wage policy is left to whatever the majority enacts; the ideology itself takes no side.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: No economic doctrine is attached to majority primacy; the question is for majorities to settle.

public-ownership.rationale: Ownership of industry is a policy choice for the majority, not a defining commitment.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: Tax levels follow what majorities choose; the ideology is indifferent in itself, though a poor majority could favour it.

unions-good.rationale: Nothing in majority primacy settles labor questions, so adherents split by their wider politics.

property-fundamental.rationale: Treating property as very hard to override is an entrenched limit on majorities, which the advocates in the Wikipedia account reject; Locke though protects property absent consent.

regulate-corporations.rationale: Regulation is an ordinary policy matter for majorities; no stated position.

cut-welfare.rationale: Welfare levels are for the majority to determine; the ideology has no stated view.

worker-ownership.rationale: Business ownership structure is not addressed by majoritarian theory.

surveillance-ok.rationale: Not addressed; adherents would defer to what a majority and its legislature approve, so split.

legalize-drugs.rationale: Left to majority preference; the ideology itself is indifferent.

restrict-hate-speech.rationale: Adherents defer to legislative majorities on speech law, while resisting court-imposed speech rights; no fixed answer.

strong-leader.rationale: Majoritarian theory centers an elected legislature and majority cabinet, though Westminster executives are strong; bypassing gridlock by a leader is not its mechanism.

state-harmful.rationale: Majoritarianism is a theory of how the state decides, assuming authority is legitimate when it rests on majority consent (Locke).

limit-guns.rationale: A policy for majorities to decide; no ideology-specific stance.

empower-police-military.rationale: Security funding is decided by majorities; no stated position.

legalize-sex-work.rationale: Left to majority choice; no stated position.

decide-locally.rationale: Lijphart's classic majoritarian model is unitary and centralised, with decentralisation appearing only in the qualified strand.

rehabilitation.rationale: Penal philosophy is not touched by majoritarian theory.

traditional-family.rationale: Social values follow the majority; adherents are split by their other commitments.

same-sex-marriage.rationale: Left to majority legislatures; adherents oppose court-imposed answers either way.

abortion-legal.rationale: Like other moral questions, for the majority to settle; no fixed stance.

more-religion-public.rationale: A religious majority could favour it (Wikipedia notes majorities may be defined by religion), but the procedural core is neutral.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: Depends on what the majority supports; no stated position.

gender-social-construct.rationale: An academic claim outside the ideology.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: The ethnic or cultural strand gives the majority group primacy, but the procedural mainstream is silent; inferred.

gradual-change.rationale: Majoritarians welcome fast change if a majority backs it, yet also oppose entrenched barriers to change; split.

reduce-immigration.rationale: Left to majority opinion; the procedural core has no stance.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: Handing power to bodies outside majority control cuts against popular majority primacy; inferred.

nation-first.rationale: Not addressed beyond deferring to the national majority; inferred split.

humanitarian-intervention.rationale: Foreign policy is not addressed by the doctrine.

open-borders.rationale: Eventual open borders would dilute a settled majority's say over membership; inferred.

tech-solves-problems.rationale: A general outlook outside the ideology.

expand-nuclear.rationale: Energy policy is for majorities to decide.

revolution-justified.rationale: Locke allows dissolving government that breaks trust, but majoritarians stress electoral change; inferred.

experts-over-public.rationale: Majoritarianism holds decisions should rest on the majority; Wikipedia contrasts it with Plato's rule by the knowledgeable few.

socialized-markets.rationale: Which firms markets may contain is an economic design choice that majority rule leaves to whichever majority forms.

state-directs-investment.rationale: Industrial strategy is ordinary legislation; the doctrine only requires that it be what the majority chose.

widespread-small-property.rationale: The pattern of property holding is not part of a decision-rule doctrine, so adherents hold no shared view.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: Abolishing money would be an extreme change, and majoritarians accept it only if a majority chose; inferred.

abolish-central-banks.rationale: Majoritarian model favours executive control of the central bank, but abolition is a different question; no position.

corporatist-bargaining.rationale: Lijphart pairs the majoritarian model with pluralist interest groups, not corporatist bodies setting wages and prices.

one-party-rule.rationale: The model is built on competitive elections and alternation, in which a majority can be replaced by another.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Westminster majoritarianism coexists with constitutional monarchy, but the ideology does not need it.

democracy-best.rationale: Advocates argue that majority decision-making is inherently democratic and that elite rule becomes oligarchy.

direct-votes.rationale: Majority decision applied directly to laws fits the doctrine, though majoritarian Westminster systems rely on parliaments.

workers-councils.rationale: Replacing parliaments with class-based councils departs from general majority rule among all citizens.

right-to-secede.rationale: Majoritarians treat the whole polity's majority as sovereign, so a regional minority leaving is not its default; inferred.

natural-rulers.rationale: The doctrine rests on equal say for the many, rejecting the Platonic case that some are fit to rule.

political-violence-never.rationale: Locke allows resistance to broken trust but majoritarians stress ballots; split.

war-builds-character.rationale: A claim about national character; majority decision-making says nothing for or against it.

separate-church-state.rationale: Neutral procedurally; a religious majority could dissent.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: A religious majority may want it, but the doctrine does not require it.

private-courts-defense.rationale: Locke places lawmaking and judging under the community acting by majority; privatisation is not part of it.

military-superiority.rationale: Defence posture is decided by the elected majority, and the doctrine has no view on how large it should be.

ethnic-nation.rationale: Ethnic majoritarianism exists, but the mainstream procedural strand is indifferent; strands split.

equal-outcomes.rationale: Equality of outcomes is a policy aim that a majority may or may not adopt, not part of majoritarian theory.

indigenous-land-authority.rationale: Special authority for a minority over territory sits awkwardly with majority decision; inferred.

civilizational-union.rationale: Unions of peoples by religion or civilization are not discussed; the doctrine concerns decisions within one community.

self-interest-moral.rationale: An ethical claim outside the doctrine.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Majoritarians tend to treat rights as what majorities enact, but the claim is about individual duty; inferred.

nature-intrinsic-value.rationale: A question of environmental ethics that majority-rule theory leaves open.

limit-population.rationale: Population policy would be set by majority legislation; the doctrine itself is silent.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: A historical judgement with no link to how decisions are made, so no shared answer.

accelerate-technology.rationale: The pace of technological change is outside majoritarian theory.

human-enhancement.rationale: Bodily freedom with technology is a matter for majority legislation, and adherents are not united on it.

algorithmic-government.rationale: Handing decisions to algorithms displaces majority decision; inferred.

unbreakable-encryption.rationale: A civil-liberties and security question left to what legislatures choose.

restore-past-order.rationale: Majoritarians accept change or restoration alike if a majority wants it, so this is not a doctrinal question.

results-over-ideology.rationale: Judging policies by results is a general stance; majoritarianism concerns who decides, not how policies are judged.

direct-action.rationale: Majoritarians route change through elections and legislatures, where majorities form.

means-match-ends.rationale: A claim about political method; majoritarians simply require majority endorsement, with no view on prefiguration.

return-to-foraging.rationale: A civilizational question wholly outside the doctrine, which would accept it only if a majority chose it.

abolish-division-of-labor.rationale: An economic-social aim not addressed by majority-rule theory.

distribute-by-need.rationale: Principles of distribution are for the majority to decide; the doctrine does not choose among them.

production-for-use.rationale: Economic organisation is outside what majoritarianism specifies.

profit-exploitation.rationale: A Marxist economic thesis that the doctrine neither affirms nor denies.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: Class rule over a former ruling class denies equal say to all citizens, contrary to rule by the majority of the people.

collective-farming.rationale: Farm organisation is an agricultural policy choice for majorities, with no doctrinal answer.

capitalism-causes-war.rationale: A theory of imperialism with no connection to majority decision procedure.

taxation-theft.rationale: Locke holds taxes need the consent of the majority or its representatives, so taxation is legitimate when so consented.

harm-principle.rationale: Majorities may legislate on matters beyond harm; the doctrine limits the majority only to keeping future majorities possible.

individual-rights-only.rationale: Majoritarians accept group-defined majorities and reject entrenched rights; unclear.

exit-over-voice.rationale: Majoritarianism prizes the vote and majority decision as the democratic check.

state-as-business.rationale: Treating citizens as customers replaces collective decision with exit; inferred.

positive-liberty.rationale: A debate about the meaning of freedom; majority-rule theory takes no side.

media-academia-power.rationale: Populist majoritarians may agree, but the doctrine does not claim it.

hereditarian-race.rationale: An empirical claim about heredity unrelated to how decisions are made.

organic-representation.rationale: Lijphart ties majoritarianism to territorial elections and party competition, not corporate representation.

total-state.rationale: Total direction conflicts with decisions resting on the majority; inferred.

national-rebirth.rationale: Rebirth narratives belong to nationalist movements; the procedural doctrine does not rely on them.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Foreign expansion is a policy a majority could choose or reject; the doctrine has no view.

bound-labor.rationale: Locke's consent basis conflicts with hereditary bound labour; inferred.

no-neutral-knowledge.rationale: An epistemological claim outside political decision procedure.

universal-morality.rationale: Majoritarians settle moral disagreement by voting, but need not deny universal truths, so no clear answer.

single-common-good.rationale: Majoritarianism settles disagreement by counting votes among competing views, not by finding one reasoned good.

jewish-state-israel.rationale: A nationalist claim concerning one nation, which general majority-rule theory does not address.

diaspora-return-right.rationale: A question of citizenship law that a national majority would decide; no doctrinal answer.

revive-national-language.rationale: Language policy is for the national majority to decide; no stated position.

workplace-democracy.rationale: Not addressed beyond favouring majority voting where used.

school-vouchers.rationale: Education funding design is ordinary policy, not touched by the doctrine.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: Fiscal policy would follow the elected majority; the doctrine has no view.

economic-freedom.rationale: A liberal claim about freedom's preconditions; majoritarianism concerns the decision rule, not this link.

rule-by-example.rationale: Moral example is not a decision procedure; majorities and laws govern.

national-self-determination.rationale: Self-rule by a nation's majority fits popular sovereignty; inferred.

force-without-un.rationale: Authorisation for force is decided by the national government and its majority, with no doctrinal rule.

reason-over-faith.rationale: An epistemic stance outside the doctrine; majorities may be religious or secular.

sacrifice-heritage.rationale: A cultural-policy question left to what a majority prefers.

workers-nation.rationale: The organising level of the working class is a socialist debate unrelated to majority rule.

patriarchy-structural.rationale: A sociological claim about society that the doctrine does not address.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: Populist strands claim it, but the doctrine does not.

heritable-defect-limits.rationale: Eugenic policy is not part of majoritarian theory, though a majority could enact it; adherents have no shared position.

security-forces-accountable.rationale: Accountability for past abuses would be decided through the legislature; the doctrine takes no stance.

night-watchman-state.rationale: The size of government is left to what majorities choose.

discourage-race-mixing.rationale: A racial-social question with no basis in the procedural doctrine.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: SEP grounds democracy partly in equality, and majority rule treats each vote equally; but legal-equality limits are not entrenched.

socialism-one-country.rationale: A debate within Marxism, unrelated to majority decision.

settler-state-colonial.rationale: A historical-political classification not addressed by the doctrine.

uniform-civil-code.rationale: Not addressed beyond a majority's preference.

restrict-conversion.rationale: Religious-majority strands might back it, but the procedural core does not address it.

ban-cattle-slaughter.rationale: Religious-majority strands may favour it; procedural core silent.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: School religion would be settled by the majority; no doctrinal answer.

state-strengthens-encirclement.rationale: A Marxist-Leninist state theory outside the doctrine.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Locke grounds government in consent and holds the act of the majority passes for the act of the whole (sect. 96).

trade-surplus.rationale: A mercantilist aim unrelated to decision procedure.

population-transfer.rationale: Wikipedia says the one acceptable limit is that a majority cannot exclude minorities from participating, which expulsion violates.

initiating-force-wrong.rationale: A libertarian ethical principle; majoritarians accept that majority decisions may be enforced on dissenters.

competition-drives-progress.rationale: A social-Darwinist or liberal claim unrelated to the doctrine.

freedom-as-non-domination.rationale: A republican theory of freedom; majoritarianism does not adopt or reject it.

separated-powers.rationale: Lijphart's majoritarian model has executive dominance of the legislature, not checks, though Locke separates powers.

vanguard-party.rationale: A minority party leading the class contradicts rule by the majority of the people.

priority-to-poor.rationale: A distributional principle left to the majority.

right-to-buy-council-homes.rationale: Housing policy decided by the majority of the day; no doctrinal answer.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: Labour law is ordinary legislation for majorities.

population-causes-poverty.rationale: A Malthusian empirical claim unrelated to the doctrine.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: Ethnic strand may claim it; procedural core silent.

offices-by-lottery.rationale: Election by majority is the standard mechanism; Waldron critics note lottery could replace judges but not elections.

price-controls-essentials.rationale: Emergency price policy is ordinary legislation, with no doctrinal answer.

party-controls-media.rationale: Competitive politics needs open contest so majorities can change; inferred.

party-commands-army.rationale: Party command of the army is one-party practice; inferred.

long-naturalization-wait.rationale: Citizenship rules would be set by the national majority; the doctrine has no view.

representatives-worker-pay.rationale: Pay of legislators is a matter for the legislature; the doctrine does not specify it.

party-discipline-binding.rationale: Westminster executive dominance rests on party discipline, but nothing makes it binding doctrine; inferred.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Pooling sovereignty moves decisions beyond a national majority; inferred.

head-commands-forces.rationale: The model has the cabinet answerable to a parliamentary majority, not a head of state commanding; inferred.

church-by-bishops.rationale: Church governance is not a question for general majoritarian theory.

clerical-rule.rationale: Rule by religious scholars is rule by a few, which advocates call oligarchy.

defeat-own-government-war.rationale: A revolutionary-socialist stance with no basis in majority-rule theory.

unlimited-reelection.rationale: If voters choose it, majoritarians accept; but not a doctrine.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: Alliance policy is for the elected majority; the doctrine does not take sides.

abolish-rental-housing.rationale: A radical property proposal not addressed by majoritarianism.

people-in-arms.rationale: Military organisation is for legislatures to decide; no doctrinal view.

rural-life-healthier.rationale: A cultural judgement unrelated to decision procedure.

reunify-divided-nation.rationale: National reunification would be decided by a majority, but the doctrine does not require it.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: A cultural-theory claim that majoritarianism does not address.

death-penalty.rationale: Capital punishment would be settled by the legislative majority; the doctrine itself takes no side.

sex-ed-in-schools.rationale: Curriculum content is left to the elected majority, and the doctrine gives no answer.

religious-exemptions.rationale: Exemptions for minorities from general laws limit what a majority enacted; inferred.

encourage-eccentricity.rationale: Mill's claim is outside the doctrine.

rich-countries-aid-poor.rationale: Aid is a spending choice for majorities; no doctrinal duty is stated.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: Not addressed; Westminster uses parliamentary selection.

central-bank-independence.rationale: Lijphart lists independent central banks on the consensus side; the majoritarian model has executive control.

no-land-for-peace.rationale: Territorial concessions are decided by the national majority, with no doctrinal answer.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: The grounds of property are left to what majorities decide; the sources do not say.

soviet-state-capitalist.rationale: A historical classification debate outside the doctrine.

precautionary-principle.rationale: Environmental regulation standards are ordinary policy for majorities.

collective-defense.rationale: A treaty design question in foreign policy beyond the doctrine.

annexed-territory-occupation.rationale: An international-law question that majoritarianism does not address.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: Church-state relations would follow the majority; no shared doctrinal view.

nonpartisan-head-of-state.rationale: Westminster systems have such heads of state, but the doctrine does not require them.

force-to-prevent-secession.rationale: A national majority treated as sovereign over the whole territory would resist its minority leaving; inferred.

region-keeps-system.rationale: Special autonomy is the decentralising qualified strand rather than the classic unitary model; inferred.

sacred-ruler.rationale: Locke's consent basis contradicts sacred authority, since authority rests on majority consent.

flat-income-tax.rationale: Tax structure is left to majorities, with no doctrinal answer.

character-from-environment.rationale: A psychological claim unrelated to political decision procedure.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Locke says the legislature cannot be arbitrary and must rule by standing laws; majoritarians locate sovereignty in the people.

space-expansion.rationale: A civilisational goal that majority-rule theory does not address.

mixed-constitution.rationale: A mix of few and many dilutes rule by the many; Wikipedia says elite rule becomes oligarchy.

leader-cult.rationale: Public honour of leaders is a cultural practice the doctrine does not address.

equal-parenting.rationale: Family-court policy would be decided by the legislature; no doctrinal view.

class-struggle-under-socialism.rationale: A Maoist theory unrelated to the doctrine.

land-redistribution.rationale: Land reform would be done if a majority chose it; the doctrine itself is silent.

ban-cartels.rationale: Competition law is ordinary regulation for majorities.

no-bailouts.rationale: Bailout policy is left to elected governments; no doctrinal answer.

gender-parity-bodies.rationale: Quotas on public bodies are not addressed; majoritarians accept only limits that keep participation open, so no clear answer.

economic-self-sufficiency.rationale: Autarky is an economic policy choice outside the doctrine.
